title: A Little Tshiluba
bodyHtml:
Tshiluba, spoken by about 6 million people, is one of the official languages of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Below are some sentences in Tshiluba, along with their English translations:

TshilubaEnglish
mukaji uvwa mumona muana.The woman saw the child.
bakaji bavwa bamona muana.The women saw the child.
muluma uvwa mumona bakaji.The man saw the women.
muluma uvwa mumona bambuji.The man saw the goats.
banzolu bavwa bamona bantambwe.The chickens saw the lions.
tubambwa tuvwa tumona baluma.The small dogs saw the men.
mbwa uvwa mumona ntambwe.The dog saw the lion.
ntambwe uvwa mumona tubanzolu.The lion saw the small chickens.
kanzolu kavwa kamona tubantambwe.The small chicken saw the small lions.
tubakulu tuvwa tumona mbwa.The small adults saw the dog.
kamuntu kavwa kapeta kantambwe.The small person found the small lion.

Answer these questions in the Answer Sheets.

A1. Translate the following into Tshiluba:

  1. the dog
  2. The man saw the child.
  3. The chicken saw the dogs.
  4. The adult found the goat.
  5. The small goats found the small child.

A2. Tshiluba belongs to a group of languages known as the Bantu languages. What does bantu mean in Tshiluba?

A3. The Tshiluba word for “fruit” is cimuma, and the Tshiluba word for “fruits” is bimuma. Translate the following into English:

  1. cimuma civwa cimona ntambwe.
  2. ntambwe uvwa mumona tubimuma.

questions.promptHtml: e. The small goats found the small child.

questions.partPrompt: Tshiluba belongs to a group of languages known as the Bantu languages. What does bantu mean in Tshiluba?
The Tshiluba word for "fruit" is cimuma, and the Tshiluba word for "fruits" is bimuma. Translate the following into English.

questions.answerKey: The lion saw the small fruits.

hints.text: Compare the first two sentences. Only the beginnings of the words change, and all three words in the sentence change together. Tshiluba marks meaning with prefixes at the front of nouns and verbs, so line up the prefixes column by column.

Each noun carries a prefix that tells you its class: mu- for one, ba- for more than one, ka- for one small thing, tu- for several small things, plus some nouns that start with a nasal like mbwa or ntambwe. Whatever prefix the subject noun has, the two verb words in the sentence copy that same prefix. The diminutive prefix ka-/tu- is added in front of the noun's own prefix rather than replacing it.

Try an ungraded example: "The small woman saw the goats." The woman is mukaji, so a single small one is ka- plus mukaji, giving kamukaji. Because the subject now begins with ka-, both verb words take ka- as well: kavwa kamona. The object "the goats" is bambuji. Put it together in subject-verb-object order and you get kamukaji kavwa kamona bambuji.

explanationHtml:
Where to start: the words all change together

Look at the first two rows:

  • mukaji uvwa mumona muana. — The woman saw the child.
  • bakaji bavwa bamona muana. — The women saw the child.

Only the fronts of the words differ: mu-kaji becomes ba-kaji, and at the same time u-vwa mu-mona becomes ba-vwa ba-mona. So Tshiluba builds words out of a stem (-kaji “woman”) plus a prefix, and the verb words repeat the subject's prefix. This repeating is called agreement.

The noun classes

Sorting the nouns gives a neat system:

onemore than onemeaning
mukajibakajiwoman / women
mulumabalumaman / men
muana(not shown)child
mbwabambwadog / dogs
nzolubanzoluchicken / chickens
ntambwebantambwelion / lions
mbujibambujigoat / goats
muntubantuperson / people
mukulubakuluadult / adults

Plurals of every one of these nouns start with ba-. That is where A2 comes from: muntu is “person” (we see kamuntu “small person”), so bantu must be the plural, “people”.

“Small” is a prefix, and it stacks

Compare bambwa “dogs” with tubambwa “small dogs”, and ntambwe “lion” with kantambwe “small lion”. “Small” is ka- for one thing and tu- for several, and it goes in front of whatever the noun already had: tu-ba-ntambwe “small lions”, tu-ba-kulu “small adults”, ka-muntu “small person”.

The verb: two words, both agreeing

Every sentence has the shape subject + -vwa + verb. The past is expressed with the little word -vwa followed by the main verb, -mona “see” or -peta “find”, and both of them wear the subject's prefix:

subject begins withverb words
mu- or a nasal (mbwa, ntambwe, nzolu)uvwa mumona
ba-bavwa bamona
tu-tuvwa tumona
ka-kavwa kamona
ci-civwa cimona

Notice that the object noun never changes shape — only the subject controls agreement. Word order is subject, verb, object, just like English.

Doing the translations

For “The adult found the goat”: tubakulu “small adults” tells us the plural is bakulu, so one adult is mukulu. A mu- subject takes uvwa plus mu- on the main verb, and “found” is -peta (from the last data sentence). The object “the goat” is mbuji.

For the sentence with small goats as the subject: “small goats” = tu- in front of the plural bambuji, and then the verbs must both take tu-. “The small child” as object is simply ka- in front of muana.

A new class in A3

cimuma / bimuma “fruit / fruits” shows a class pair ci- / bi- that did not appear in the main data. But the same rules apply: a ci- subject gives civwa cimona, and tu-bimuma is “small fruits”, the diminutive stacked on the plural, exactly like tubantambwe.

These stacking noun-class prefixes with agreement all through the sentence are the trademark of the Bantu family — the family whose name is literally the Tshiluba word for “people.”
